venereus (venerius), venerea, venereum

of sexual love, sexual

From Venus: rēs venereae are sex, voluptātēs venereae sexual pleasures. Its first sense is “of Venus” (her priests, her temple slaves), and at dice the Venus throw. Sexual desire is libīdō or venus (Plin.; M-O s.v. sex drive).

Other words

  • sexuālis, sexuāle — of sex; in its one ancient use, of a woman

    declension · also used · late Latin · Cael. Aur. Acut. 3.17: manus, a woman’s hand (Lewis & Short)

    Late and rare (Lewis & Short), and there it means “of the female sex”, from sexus; the modern sense comes from the modern languages. Clear, but venereus is the classical word.

Examples

  • Bene Sophoclēs, cum ex eō quīdam jam affectō aetāte quaereret, ūterēturne rēbus veneriīs, «Dī meliōra!» inquit.

    Sophocles answered well when someone asked him, already an old man, whether he still had sex: “Heaven forbid!”Cic. Sen. 47

  • prīdiē castus ab rēbus veneriīs neve tēmulentus nec nisi lōtus ad eās accēdat

    the day before, let him keep from sex, not be drunk, and not go near them (the hives) without washingCol. 9.14.3

See also sex, sex, love.
